name: Isosurface extraction
text:
# Isosurface extraction

Also called: Marching Cubes family, contouring, polygonization

## Overview
Isosurface extraction converts a discretized scalar field into a polygonal mesh (typically triangles) representing the surface where the scalar value equals a specified isovalue [S1, S4, unofficial]. It solves the problem of visualizing implicit 3D structures by approximating the continuous zero-level set with a discrete manifold. Unlike [Blocky meshing](31-blocky-meshing.md), which produces voxel-aligned "blocky" geometry based on occupancy states, isosurface methods generate smooth, curved surfaces by interpolating between grid vertices [S1, S4, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md) (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers. The core mechanism involves traversing the grid cells and evaluating the data to determine which parts of the domain constitute the surface.

1.  **Domain Traversal**: The algorithm iterates over the volume data structure. For [regular grids](#3-dense-grids-and-memory-layout.md), this often involves checking each cell or voxel.
2.  **Surface Determination**: A criterion is applied to identify surface locations. In isosurface methods, this involves comparing scalar values against a threshold (isovalue) to detect sign changes or equality [30-isosurface-extraction.md]. In [blocky meshing](#31-blocky-meshing.md), this involves checking occupancy states or material IDs to identify exposed boundaries [31-blocky-meshing.md].
3.  **Primitive Generation**: Geometric primitives (vertices, edges, faces) are generated based on the determined surface locations.
4.  **Mesh Coherence**: Adjacent primitives are merged or connected to form a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates and ensure watertightness [30-isosurface-extraction.md].

## Subtopics

### [Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces](819-advancing-front-framework-for-implicit-surfaces.md)
Constructs a triangulated mesh by growing a front across the implicit surface, starting from a seed point and extending it edge-by-edge. Unlike grid-based methods such as [Marching Cubes](30-isosurface-extraction.md) or [Marching Tetrahedra](30-isosurface-extraction.md) which traverse a discretized domain to determine topology locally, this method operates without a pre-defined volume description, requiring the algorithm to discover and chart the surface geometry dynamically. It is distinguished by its ability to generate high-quality, well-shaped triangles directly, avoiding the post-processing often required by topological grid methods, though it is computationally more intensive.

### [MLS Projection](823-mls-projection.md)
Iterative algorithm that projects a query point onto a surface defined by a set of input points and their associated normals using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation. It solves the problem of reconstructing smooth, noise-resistant implicit surfaces from unorganized point clouds by fitting local quadratic functions to the Hermite data (positions and normals). It sets itself apart from standard isosurface extraction methods like [Marching Cubes](30-isosurface-extraction.md) by operating directly on point sets rather than grid samples, and from [Dual Contouring](778-dual-contouring.md) by explicitly computing a projected point and normal via iterative tangent plane averaging rather than optimizing a vertex position via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF).

### [Isosurface Extraction API](836-isosurface-extraction-api.md)
Provides a high-level interface for extracting a manifold triangular mesh from a continuous implicit scalar field defined by a user-supplied function, rather than a pre-computed discrete grid. It solves the problem of converting mathematical implicit surfaces into polygonal meshes by internally managing an adaptive [octree traversal](#1587-octree-traversal.md) and calling a Rust-based core extraction routine. It sets itself apart from standard grid-based methods like [Marching Cubes](30-isosurface-extraction.md) by accepting a callable function `func(x,y,z)` directly, handling gradient estimation via finite differences if not provided, and supporting adaptive refinement through octree depth parameters.

### [Minimal Area Triangulation for Polygons](859-minimal-area-triangulation-for-polygons.md)
Converts complex, non-convex 3D polygons (isopolygons) resulting from isosurface extraction into a set of triangles by minimizing the total surface area of the resulting mesh. It solves the problem of generating a high-quality, artifact-free mesh from the closed loops formed by intersecting an implicit field with octree nodes. Unlike standard triangulation methods that may produce self-intersecting or visually noisy surfaces, this method leverages the geometric property that isopolygons lie on the boundary of convex bodies (octree nodes) to guarantee a homeomorphic-to-disk triangulation that is minimal in area. It is distinct from sibling methods like [Dual Contouring](778-dual-contouring.md) which optimize vertex positions via QEF, and [Surface Nets](921-surface-nets.md) which use cell centers, by strictly optimizing the connectivity of existing intersection vertices to minimize geometric error.

### [VESTA](900-vesta.md)
Constructs isosurfaces by generating N-cycles from 3-cell configurations, resolving ambiguities at voxel face junctures to prevent surface holes, unlike the original [Marching Cubes Algorithm](#777-marching-cubes.md). It is a volume-enclosing [surface extraction](#29-surface-extraction.md) algorithm that processes voxel face vectors (VFVs) to generate a closed, oriented surface composed of triangles (3-cycles). It handles both isolated voxels and complex connected shapes by establishing connectivity through boundary face centers and junctures. Unlike template-based methods like Marching Cubes, [VESTA](#900-vesta.md) uses a single building block based on vector decomposition of a single voxel face to resolve 3D cell ambiguities without generating holes.

### [Isosurface extraction on arbitrary polyhedral grids](951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md)
Extracts isosurfaces from scalar fields defined on arbitrary polyhedral cells (convex, non-convex, planar, or non-planar) by treating face boundaries systematically to avoid the topological inconsistencies inherent in standard Marching Cubes on ambiguous faces. It approximates the isosurface locally at each cell as a polygonal surface (isopolygon) using a [general polygon tracing procedure](#951-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-polyhedral-grids.md) that does not rely on predefined [configuration tables](#1484-marching-cubes-face-generation.md) or cell decomposition. Unlike Marching Cubes, which suffers from holes and non-2-manifold surfaces in ambiguous configurations, this method ensures consistent results by sequentially joining intersection points on cell edges based on strict inequality rules.

### [Extended CLCIR PLIC Reconstruction](954-extended-clcir-plic-reconstruction.md)
Reconstructs a Piecewise Linear Interface Concept (PLIC) plane for Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations on arbitrary polyhedral grids by extracting an isosurface from an interpolated scalar field and computing a weighted normal vector. It distinguishes itself from standard VOF reconstruction methods by explicitly using isosurface extraction to handle non-convex and self-intersecting polyhedral cells without decomposition, and from pure isosurface methods by its explicit geometric flux calculation and volume conservation enforcement. It builds on [Isosurface extraction](30-isosurface-extraction.md) to determine the interface geometry.

### [Multi-Isosurface Extraction](1162-multi-isosurface-extraction.md)
Extracts and renders multiple isosurfaces from the same scalar volume data simultaneously by running the Marching Cubes algorithm for each selected isovalue. Unlike single isosurface extraction, this method requires managing multiple triangle lists and potentially multiple rendering passes or state changes for different isovalue colors. It builds on [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md) by extending the extraction loop to iterate over a user-defined list of isovalues rather than a single scalar threshold.

### [Convex Contouring with Decision Trees](1201-convex-contouring-with-decision-trees.md)
A table-driven isosurface extraction technique that generates topologically consistent surfaces where the negative space inside each cell is convex. Unlike [Marching Cubes](30-isosurface-extraction.md), which may produce disconnected or non-convex negative space, this method ensures that the polygonal contour inside each cell encloses a convex hull of negative corners and edge intersections. This convexity property enables fast collision detection on the triangulated isosurface. The method distinguishes itself by using pre-computed decision trees to dynamically select the correct triangulation from a set of candidates based on the exact positions of edge intersections, rather than relying solely on vertex signs.

### [Octree-based Isosurfacing](1247-octree-based-isosurfacing.md)
Replaces the uniform Cartesian grid of standard methods like [Marching Cubes](30-isosurface-extraction.md) with an adaptive octree spatial discretization. This allows the resolution to adapt to the complexity of the implicit scalar field, reducing memory usage and computation time for sparse or complex data. Unlike uniform grid approaches, it lacks inherent topological guarantees; specifically, if the octree is not sufficiently refined or adapted to the surface geometry, topological cracks can appear in the resulting mesh, particularly when using Marching Cubes.

### [High-Dimensional Triangulation Tables](1336-high-dimensional-triangulation-tables.md)
Generates [precomputed triangulation tables](#4800-marching-cubes-lookup-table.md) for isosurface extraction in $n$-dimensional hypercubes. It addresses the excessive simplex count produced by recursive contour-meshing, which requires subdividing 4-cells into 4-simplices before contouring. Unlike recursive contour-meshing, which creates more triangles than the Marching Cubes algorithm, this method uses a lookup table similar to Marching Cubes but generalized for any $n$-dimensional hypercube.

### [Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra](1737-subgrid-marching-tetrahedra.md)
Reconstructs an intersection-free triangulation by decomposing a regular cubic grid into tetrahedra and resolving the scalar field crossings within each tetrahedron. Unlike its sibling [Marching Cubes](4328-naive-isosurface-extraction.md), which suffers from topological ambiguities in specific configurations, this method guarantees a manifold, self-intersection-free surface by enforcing a consistent local construction policy based on edge intersection counts. It produces a mesh that matches voxel data more accurately than Marching Cubes, at the cost of a higher vertex count.

### [Optimized Mesh Reference](1888-optimized-mesh-reference.md)
A theoretical performance baseline for indirect isosurface visualization, representing the best-case scenario where an explicit mesh is rendered with zero overhead for geometry extraction or occlusion culling. It serves to measure the theoretical upper bound of rendering performance by evaluating a highly-optimized explicit mesh representation, allowing researchers to assess how close a proposed pipeline comes to the ideal efficiency of forward mesh rendering. Unlike direct ray-marching references, it isolates the rasterization cost of an already-extracted and optimized surface.

### [Snap Marching Cubes](2181-snap-marching-cubes.md)
Improves mesh quality by reducing the number of triangles and eliminating small angles, which are common artifacts in standard Marching Cubes. It achieves this by modifying the scalar field to "snap" isosurface vertices that are geometrically close to grid vertices onto those grid vertices, causing nearby geometric elements to merge. Unlike adaptive methods such as [Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces](819-advancing-front-framework-for-implicit-surfaces.md) or [DelIso](954-extended-clcir-plic-reconstruction.md), SnapMC is non-adaptive and operates on a uniform grid, offering a significant speedup over adaptive counterparts at the cost of potential topological errors and non-manifold surfaces.

### [Hybrid Memory Constrained Isosurface Extraction](2307-hybrid-memory-constrained-isosurface-extraction.md)
Generates isosurfaces from regularly structured volume data while strictly respecting a prescribed memory limit $M$ for auxiliary data structures. It solves the problem of minimizing the expected extraction time $E[T]$ by optimally partitioning the volume spatially and assigning one of several constituent search methods (enumeration, interval tree, kd-tree, or out-of-core) to each partition block. Unlike standard marching cubes which stores the entire mesh or pure streaming methods that may produce artifacts, this method uses Lagrangian optimization to select an optimal partition tree and extraction methods for its nodes, maximizing [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) under the memory constraint.

### [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md)
Provides the static data structures and mapping logic that determine how a voxel's scalar field [sign configuration](#3639-cube-sdf-sampling-and-sign-configuration.md) is converted into mesh geometry. It solves the combinatorial problem of isosurface extraction by replacing runtime conditional branching with direct array indexing, enabling $O(1)$ determination of triangle topology per voxel. It differs from symmetry-based approaches by handling all 256 cases explicitly (or via symmetry reduction) and from dynamic ambiguity resolution methods by using fixed triangulations for ambiguous cases, which may produce topological artifacts if adjacent cells resolve ambiguities inconsistently.

### [Surface Properties and Estimation](2790-surface-properties-and-estimation.md)
Provides methods to compute geometric attributes (normals, area) or improve the visual quality (smoothing) of isosurfaces extracted via algorithms like Marching Cubes. It differs from the extraction algorithms themselves by operating either on the input scalar field to improve extraction quality or on the resulting mesh to compute derived properties.

### [General-purpose Contour Extraction Routine Generator](3666-general-purpose-contour-extraction-routine-generator.md)
A code generator that produces a JavaScript function to extract surfaces from multi-dimensional `ndarray` data structures. It solves the problem of traversing a discretized domain and generating vertices and faces based on phase comparisons between adjacent grid cells. It differs from static isosurface algorithms (like Marching Cubes) by being a meta-algorithm: it accepts callbacks for phase evaluation, vertex creation, and cell (face) creation, allowing the user to define arbitrary topological rules and output formats rather than being restricted to a fixed triangulation scheme.

### [Surface Tessellation from Iso-Contours](3696-surface-tessellation-from-iso-contours.md)
Represents volumetric data by generating polygonal surfaces from stacks of 2D contours located on consecutive slices of parallel planes within a data volume. Unlike cell-based methods like Marching Cubes that operate on discrete grid cells, this approach operates on the topological relationship between adjacent 2D contour loops. It is primarily distinguished by its reliance on pre-extracted 2D contours and the specific challenge of triangulating the "ribbon" of surface area between two such contours, often requiring user [interaction](#41-interaction.md) or complex optimization to resolve ambiguities when multiple contours exist on a single slice.

### [THREAD System](3743-thread-system.md)
An early surface extraction method that reconstructs 3D geometry from a sequence of 2D cross-sectional images by tessellating between outlines on consecutive slices. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures (such as medical anatomy) by creating a polygonal mesh from segmented 2D boundaries, differing from grid-based isosurface extraction methods like Marching Cubes by operating directly on discrete slice contours rather than a volumetric scalar field.

### [Simplified Marching Cubes](3759-simplified-marching-cubes.md)
Produces meshes using only vertices from the regular 3D grid, eliminating interpolation and lookup tables. It generates approximately half the vertices and triangles of standard Marching Cubes (MC) and Cuberille, reducing memory usage by 50% while maintaining manifold topology. Unlike MC, SMC uses integer arithmetic exclusively and analyzes cube configurations independently via cumulative coordinates.

### [Preprocessed Marching Cubes](3765-preprocessed-marching-cubes.md)
Extracts a triangle mesh from a 3D scalar volume by applying optional preprocessing steps—such as Gaussian smoothing, connected-component filtering, and edge darkening—before running the standard Marching Cubes algorithm. It is designed to isolate the largest object, fill internal bubbles, and improve surface boundary detection in noisy or fragmented data. Unlike standard Marching Cubes, which may produce fragmented meshes or miss boundary details, this method ensures topological consistency and robust boundary handling through explicit preprocessing and post-processing stages.

### [Marching Cubes with Gaussian Deformation](3769-marching-cubes-with-gaussian-deformation.md)
Extracts an isosurface from a 3D scalar field using a GPU [geometry shader](#4369-geometry-shader-quads.md), applying a real-time Gaussian-based deformation to the resulting mesh vertices based on a user-defined force vector. It differs from standard GPU Marching Cubes implementations by integrating the deformation calculation directly into the geometry shader's primitive generation loop, allowing for dynamic, brush-like sculpting of the terrain during rendering. Unlike methods that rely on compute shaders for pre-processing or atomic counters for output buffering, this approach processes voxel primitives directly, discarding empty cubes early and emitting triangles on-the-fly.

### [DCX Mesh Extraction via UDF and Marching Cubes](3778-dcx-mesh-extraction-via-udf-and-marching-cubes.md)
Extracts a triangular mesh from a BVH ([Bounding Volume Hierarchy](#2808-domain-based-bvh-with-range-bounding-boxes.md)) structure by computing an Unsigned Distance Field (UDF) on a regular grid, converting it to a Signed Distance Field ([SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md)) via flood fill, and applying Marching Cubes. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by deriving the scalar field from geometric primitives via BVH queries rather than volumetric data, and from Dual Contouring by using a uniform grid with topological correction via flood fill instead of adaptive quadric optimization.

### [GPU Marching Cubes Terrain Pipeline with Indirect Rendering](3803-gpu-marching-cubes-terrain-pipeline-with-indirect-rendering.md)
Generates terrain meshes from voxel data on the GPU using Marching Cubes, utilizing indirect rendering to allow the GPU to generate and render the mesh directly without CPU readback, avoiding performance stalls. It manages multiple LOD levels and renders generated triangles via indirect draw calls to minimize CPU-GPU synchronization overhead. Unlike CPU implementations or earlier GPU versions that required reading back vertex counts or mesh data to the CPU, this pipeline keeps the RenderThread time low (~1.5ms) by keeping all draw argument generation on the GPU.

### [GPU-accelerated Marching Cubes with Distance Extraction](3818-gpu-accelerated-marching-cubes-with-distance-extraction.md)
Extracts a triangle mesh (STL) from a Signed Distance Function (SDF) by offloading the scalar field evaluation to the GPU while performing the topological marching cubes logic on the CPU. It differs from pure GPU implementations by extracting vertex distances via a fragment shader read-back to minimize GPU/CPU round-trip latency, which was found to be slower than this hybrid approach. It builds on [GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines](4136-gpu-acceleration-and-parallel-pipelines.md) by utilizing the shared principle of grid sampling but replaces parallel atomic/histogram output buffering with a CPU-side worker pool processing pre-extracted data blocks.

### [Ground Truth Generation for Neural Marching Cubes](3820-ground-truth-generation-for-neural-marching-cubes.md)
Generates the supervised training data (ground truth) required to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to predict Marching Cubes (MC) configurations for implicit surfaces, as introduced in Neural Marching Cubes (NMC). It solves the problem of mapping high-resolution surface representations (voxels and intersection points) to the discrete and continuous parameters expected by the MC algorithm for each grid cell. It differs from standard isosurface extraction by producing a multi-resolution dataset (LOD) stored in HDF5, rather than a single mesh, enabling the network to learn both topological case IDs and geometric vertex/plane parameters.

### [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md)
Generates a triangle mesh from a sparse set of 3D points with scalar values (e.g., Signed Distance Fields), avoiding the memory overhead of dense 3D grids. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by dynamically gathering corner values for active voxels via lookup, rather than iterating over a fixed dense volume. It builds on [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md).

### [Marching Cubes with Narrow-Band Filtering](3826-marching-cubes-with-narrow-band-filtering.md)
Reconstructs a triangle mesh from a signed distance function (SDF) by evaluating the SDF on a grid of cubes, filtering cubes based on distance to the surface (narrow-band), and applying the Marching Cubes algorithm to intersected cubes. It builds on [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md) by adding a spatial culling step that excludes cubes far from the surface, significantly reducing the number of cells processed.

### [Marching Cubes with QEF Vertex Optimization](3831-marching-cubes-with-qef-vertex-optimization.md)
Computes vertex positions using a Quadric Error Function (QEF) minimization for ambiguous cases, while using a 2D linear/binomial search for non-ambiguous cases, to produce a watertight mesh from a voxel grid. It distinguishes itself from standard Marching Cubes by replacing the linear interpolation of vertex positions with geometric optimization in topologically ambiguous regions, thereby reducing artifacts and improving surface fidelity without the computational overhead of full dual contouring.

### [Domain Search Isosurface Extraction](3871-domain-search-isosurface-extraction.md)
A tetrahedral marching method that extracts an isosurface from a volumetric scalar field by decomposing the domain into tetrahedra and determining intersection points via linear interpolation. It differs from cubic grid methods like Marching Cubes by operating directly on tetrahedral cells, avoiding the ambiguity issues associated with cubic cell configurations, while maintaining a straightforward lookup-table-based topology determination.

### [Modified Marching Cubes with Triangle Decimation](3903-modified-marching-cubes-with-triangle-decimation.md)
Generates an isosurface from 3D scalar field data by applying a modified marching cubes algorithm that resolves topological ambiguities and subsequently reduces polygon count via triangle decimation. It distinguishes itself from standard marching cubes by explicitly handling ambiguous cases to ensure manifold correctness and by post-processing the mesh to collapse degenerate triangles, thereby reducing storage requirements and improving visual quality.

### [Digital Surface Extraction via Khalimsky Space](3937-digital-surface-extraction-via-khalimsky-space.md)
Extracts a boundary surface from a digital image by constructing a Khalimsky space, defining a digital set based on intensity thresholds, and scanning the space to identify surfels (surface elements) using a specific adjacency rule. It differs from standard marching cubes by operating on the combinatorial manifold structure of digital surfaces rather than interpolating within grid cells, ensuring a topologically correct manifold without the ambiguity of cell configurations. It builds on [Isosurface extraction](30-isosurface-extraction.md) by replacing the geometric interpolation step with a discrete boundary scanning process.

### [Incremental Contouring via Power Diagrams](4955-incremental-contouring-via-power-diagrams.md)
Extracts an isosurface from a signed distance function by constructing a weighted triangulation (regular/power diagram or standard Delaunay) of grid samples, then incrementally refining the sample set based on geometric criteria before extracting the mesh.

### [Gallagher-Nagtegaal Bicubic Method](5321-gallagher-nagtegaal-bicubic-method.md)

### [Ray Tracing and Ray Intersection Methods](5617-ray-tracing-and-ray-intersection-methods.md)
Computes the intersection between a ray and an implicit isosurface defined by a scalar volume, returning the precise parameter $t$ where the scalar field equals the isovalue. Unlike grid-based polygonization methods that generate a mesh of primitives, these methods provide exact surface locations per ray, enabling high-quality rendering without topological artifacts. They are distinguished from [Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction](1316-binary-search-isosurface-extraction.md) by using analytical root finding (e.g., solving cubic equations) rather than iterative bisection, and from [Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing](3832-hybrid-implicit-isosurface-ray-tracing.md) by their specific handling of the trilinear interpolant within a single voxel.

### [Streaming Marching Cubes](6190-streaming-marching-cubes.md)
With [Hash Table Vertex Sharing](#6190-streaming-marching-cubes.md) is a method for extracting isosurfaces from large volumetric datasets that combines memory-efficient streaming processing with explicit vertex sharing to ensure topological consistency. It solves the problem of generating watertight, shared-vertex meshes from massive data that cannot fit entirely in memory, while avoiding the vertex duplication common in naive streaming implementations. It differs from standard [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md) by explicitly managing vertex identity across cell boundaries via a hash table, and from [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md) by focusing on the streaming memory constraint rather than spatial sparsity.

### [Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction](6315-screened-poisson-surface-reconstruction.md)

### [Dual Contouring and Surface Nets](6319-dual-contouring-and-surface-nets.md)
Generate a single vertex per active grid cell (voxel) rather than placing vertices on cell edges like Marching Cubes. This family prioritizes mesh sparsity and feature preservation over topological simplicity, producing watertight meshes with fewer triangles. Dual Contouring optimizes vertex position via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to preserve sharp features, while Surface Nets uses a weighted average of intersection points for a faster, normal-free approximation.

### [Neural and Learning-based Extraction](6371-neural-and-learning-based-extraction.md)
Generates isosurfaces from [implicit fields](#13-procedural-and-implicit-volumes.md) learned by neural networks (e.g., [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md), DVR, SDF networks) by integrating the extraction process into the optimization loop or using [adaptive sampling strategies](#1385-adaptive-sampling.md). Unlike static methods like [Marching Cubes](30-isosurface-extraction.md) or [Surface Nets](921-surface-nets.md) that operate on a fixed grid, these methods allow the mesh topology and geometry to be refined via backpropagation, enabling direct optimization of visual, geometric, or physical objectives. It sets itself apart from siblings by treating the isosurface extraction as a differentiable operation or an adaptive query process, rather than a post-processing step on a discretized volume.

#### 2+D Pen-and-Ink for Volume Visualization
A method where 2D strokes are generated based on 3D information associated with original 3D objects, treating isosurfaces as opaque objects for image buffer generation [S6, unofficial]. It extracts isosurfaces from the raw dataset, treats them as opaque objects for the generation of image buffers (lighting, depth, normals, curvature), and uses these buffers as inputs to pen-and-ink filters to synthesize a final image [S6, unofficial].

#### Point Cloud Extraction
A technique to convert isosurfaces to point clouds by evaluating chunks of voxels and extracting vertices at the center of edges where the isosurface passes, without generating face data [S7, unofficial]. It traverses the primal grid, classifies corners using a cube index, and if the index is not 0 or 255, calculates the point by linearly interpolating between corners at 0.5 [S7, unofficial]. Unlike surface reconstruction methods, this method does not contain any surface data; surfaces have to be reconstructed, ideally on the GPU itself [S7, unofficial].

#### Fast Marching-Cubes-Style Volume Evaluation
An efficient and accurate volume evaluation method for grid-based level sets that computes the volume of implicitly represented shapes consistent with Marching Cubes surface reconstruction [S8, unofficial]. It utilizes rotational symmetry to combine redundant Marching Cubes cases, avoids explicitly forming local triangulations, and uses efficient volume computation formulae for pyramids and truncated prisms wherever possible [S8, unofficial]. The method achieves second-order accuracy convergence and results perfectly consistent with volumes calculated directly from explicit Marching Cubes meshes [S8, unofficial].

#### Chunk-based Marching Cubes Update Loop
Regenerates meshes for a 3x3x3 neighborhood of voxel chunks after local noise modifications, ensuring visual continuity across chunk boundaries [S9, unofficial]. It validates that the target chunk coordinates are strictly inside the map bounds, iterates through the 3x3x3 grid, resets chunk mesh data, calls MarchThroughChunk to polygonize the chunk's noise data into a mesh using Marching Cubes, and draws the newly generated chunk mesh [S9, unofficial].

#### Mask-based Cutaways
A strategy for making inner contour surfaces visible by specifying which cells contribute to the contour surface using a mask [S10]. Only cells for which the mask value is true at all eight vertices contribute to the contour surface. The mask argument can also specify separate masks for each level as a list of logical arrays or functions [S10].

#### Radiance Mesh Extraction
Converts a tetrahedral radiance mesh into a polygonal surface mesh by filtering and grouping tetrahedra based on their visual contribution [S11, unofficial]. It measures the peak color contribution of each tetrahedron across all pixels and all training views, thresholds the radiance mesh by removing tetrahedra with a peak color contribution smaller than 0.1, identifies connected components of the remaining tetrahedra, and constructs a surface mesh for each connected component [S11, unofficial]. It uses peak color contribution across views/pixels as the filtering metric instead of geometric density, opacity, or gradient magnitude [S11, unofficial].

#### Marching Cubes on Structured Grids
Performs the marching cubes algorithm in the IJK Coordinate space and interpolates the results back into XYZ space to extract to any 3-D structured grid [S12]. The IJK-to-XYZ interpolation is not technically correct, but for most applications the difference is negligible [S12].

## Background
The Marching Cubes algorithm was introduced by William Lorensen and Harvey Cline in 1987 [S2, S4, unofficial]. It is a general approach covering a whole family of algorithms, including adaptive methods, those with sharp feature detection, and those preserving non-manifold topology [S1, S4, unofficial]. The core concept involves measuring function signs in every corner for each cell and adding line segments accordingly, connecting sign-changing edges to form a continuous contour [S4, unofficial]. Linear interpolation is used to find better places for segment ends on edges, though it is an approximation since the target function is not necessarily linear [S4, unofficial]. The error of the simple contour (middle-to-middle) never exceeds half of the cell's diagonal [S4, unofficial].
